extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, critics, and connoisseurs
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging or producing truthful and effective color, light, and atmospheric effects in landscape painting, with emphasis on fidelity to nature, handling of light and shade, and tasteful use of pure color. Geared toward painters and critics assessing technical and aesthetic correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of color (close comparison with nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is only to be measured by close comparison of actual facts; compare works with the known and demonstrable hues of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on impression, sentiment, or memory when judging color; verify by direct comparison with natural objects and effects. Ruskin insists 'we may talk forever about it in generals, and prove nothing' — only close, empirical comparison will determine truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply vivid color only where nature provides it
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use brilliancy of color on objects 'to which it does not properly belong'; vividness must correspond to nature's distribution of hue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a painter places intense hues where nature would not, the work is false. Compare masters: Turner uses vivid color where nature uses it; others (e.g., Salvator, Titian in certain cases) sometimes misapply pure hues to near, detailed objects, producing preposterous falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric perspective: reserve pure blue for air/distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Blue indicates atmosphere/air and should not be used for objects near enough to show details; 'mountains only can become pure blue when there is so much air between us and them that they become mere flat, dark shades.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid painting detailed near hills or objects in 'pure sky blue.' If details are visible, the color must show variety and warmth—blue should be used for misty distance and not detailed foreground masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotonous/unvaried color
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not one of nature's shadows, tints, or lines that is not in a state of perpetual variation; 'wherever in a painting we have unvaried color extended even over a small space, there is falsehood.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce subtle local variations—shadows, half-lights, faint warm touches—across every surface. Large, unbroken swathes of a single unmixed tone are unnatural and therefore false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate color to light and shade (chiaroscuro)
rubrics_metrics.description: Color must be entirely subordinate to arranged light and shade; 'he paints in color, but he thinks in light and shade.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the composition's chiaroscuro relationships. No hue, however rich, should be allowed to disrupt the integrity of a designed light or a determined shadow. Engravings from works with sound chiaroscuro retain force even without their original color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base tones on gray and harmonized undercurrent
rubrics_metrics.description: A general system and undercurrent of gray should pervade the color; even vivid hues are warmed or grayed so that 'there is a basis of gray, under all his vivid hues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid broad unconnected pure colors; warm blues with gray, deepen crimsons with black or yellow as modifier. This harmonizing gray makes local pure touches readable by opposition and avoids rawness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pure/raw color sparingly as key‑notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure color should appear only in concentrated, limited 'key-notes'—a single stroke or small point—rather than spread widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve the purest pigments for small decisive accents that act as the key-note of the whole composition; the rest of the canvas should be built from modified and connected tones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical verification by matching painted color to real objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Test the painting's colors against actual leaves, grass, or other natural samples to judge truth; Ruskin suggests placing 'a matched color' beside the painting and a blade of grass beside it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct side-by-side tests to detect falsehoods (e.g., compare a painted tree or foreground with a real leaf in sunlight). This exposes errors not evident by memory or abstract judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address discrepancy with light, not by lowering color
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the painter cannot reproduce nature's dazzling light, the aim should be to 'do away with this discrepancy ... not by lowering his color, but by increasing his light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to convey greater illumination and graduated illumination across the scene instead of simply desaturating or muting colors to seem 'true.' Make light the vehicle by which intense color reads as plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent extraordinary natural phenomena faithfully (e.g., sunsets)
rubrics_metrics.description: When nature 'takes a coloring fit' (such as high-cloud sunsets), the painter should follow her even if memory and common experience make observers incredulous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that certain effects occur very rarely and briefly and that viewers' memories will understate their intensity. Do not timidly reduce the effect to satisfy common prejudice; depict the extraordinary intensity and harmony present in the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible translation/substitution of tone when direct reproduction impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be acceptable to 'translate the unattainable intensity of one tone ... into the attainable pitch of a higher one' in small passages when no pigment can faithfully reproduce a given natural intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tone substitution sparingly and locally (e.g., representing golden-green sunlight by pure yellow in very small areas) and always aim to preserve light-and-shade relationships; do not broadly substitute to cover ignorance of natural values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and blending: every small area should change
rubrics_metrics.description: Never give a quarter of an inch of canvas without a change in it; nature 'varies the most general and simple of her tones' and every tuft, stone, or leaf has its own voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice minute modulation and blending across surfaces—black shadows, green shadows, gray half-lights, faint warm edges—so that even apparently simple masses contain a melody of variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on purple dominance; favor yellow-and-black opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A prevalence of purple often signals vicious color; nature generally mixes yellow into hues and favors the opposition of yellow and black (moving into white and blue) as a fundamental scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of general purple tonality; analyze whether a composition lacks yellow and therefore departs from natural tonality. Turner favors black-and-yellow foundations rather than pervasive purple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not present faded or systematized falsehoods; give only what art can truthfully state
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter should not supply a 'faded and feeble image' that seems right because of systematized falsehood; instead give completely the truths art can offer and leave the rest to the viewer's imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be honest about the limits of paint and viewing conditions. Rather than fake the full effect of nature by compositional cheats, present attainable truths (color, tone, local effect) in a way that allows an informed viewer to supply the missing impressions from memory.
